summary: Vivek Trivedy presents a recipe for continuously improving agents through data mining of trace data. The core loop: ship the agent, collect large volumes of traces, mine that data for insights, and run data-driven experiments on new prompts, tools, orchestration, or loops. He argues observability and continual learning are tightly coupled—agents produce trace data by acting in environments, and that record is the only real substrate for improvement. Unlike code, agents are difficult to reason about statically because they involve prompts, tools, skills, hooks, middlewares, and multi-agent orchestration, and prompt changes affect behavior differently across domains. LangChain sends agents to read traces from other agents, asking questions like where users got upset, whether the agent degrades after compaction events, and how a different model would perform on the same step. He emphasizes that today's data is the smallest humans will ever see, as agent-generated data will rapidly eclipse human-produced data. Key challenges include reading traces at scale being expensive and long traces not fitting in context. Open models have reached an inflection point—working with Harvey on a legal benchmark, LangChain matched Opus-level trace judging with an open model at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost through harness engineering. The iterative workflow: exhaust harness engineering (fast feedback in about two minutes), then fine-tune to break through the intelligence ceiling, then return to harness engineering. He draws an analogy to scikit-learn's fit function, describing a model-harness-task fit where the jobs become finding good fit functions (auto research, RL methods) and finding good data. Dense feedback signals are what agents lack most—benchmarks returning only pass or fail give agents nothing to act on, while traces hold fine-grained signal. He argues you can describe an agent's behavior by showing the evals it was measured against, because agents hill-climb those evals. Continual learning requires updating agent state across three axes: collecting observational training data, evolving harnesses over time, and managing memory that is not merely append-only. He points to scaling sleep-time compute and dreaming—reading traces over the entire agent life cycle to update agent state. LangSplat engine automates the trace mining loop, and outputs include distillation from good traces to smaller models and generating evals that define agent behavior.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: My agent made mistakes, now what
sections.summary: Trivedy introduces the talk's theme: improving agents is a data mining problem. The recipe is ship the agent, collect tons of traces, mine that data, then run data-driven experiments on new prompts, tools, orchestration, or loops.

sections.title: Observability and continual learning are the same problem
sections.summary: He argues observability and continual learning are tightly coupled. Agents produce trace data by acting in environments, and continual learning means updating knowledge based on feedback from that data. If you have traces, you can do continual learning.

sections.title: Why agents are harder to reason about than code
sections.summary: Unlike code, agents involve prompts, tools, skills, hooks, middlewares, and multi-agent swarms, making it hard to predict how prompt changes affect behavior at scale. Domain differences matter—a medical prompt change differs from a legal one. We are trading determinism for autonomy.

sections.title: Sending agents to read other agents' traces
sections.summary: LangChain centralizes trace data and sends agents to read traces from other agents. They look for good and bad interactions, user sentiment, whether agents degrade after compaction events, and counterfactual model comparisons. Trace-level data captures fine-grained behavior users actually see.

sections.title: Today's data is the least we will ever have
sections.summary: Agent-generated data will rapidly eclipse human-produced data. Two key challenges: reading traces at scale is expensive (input token cost times trace count times trace size), and long traces may not fit in context, requiring systems that treat trace context as an external queryable object.

sections.title: Matching frontier trace judging with an open model
sections.summary: Open models have hit an inflection point. LangChain no longer reaches for frontier models for every task. Working with Harvey on a legal benchmark, they matched Opus trace judging with an open model at 1-2 orders of magnitude cheaper through harness engineering informed by reading traces. Fine-tuning on narrow verticals can match and exceed frontier performance. Moving from token costs to hardware clusters can be cheaper for high-inference workloads.

sections.title: LangSplat engine and distillation from good traces
sections.summary: LangSplat engine automates the trace mining loop: reads trace data, finds issues, generates evals, prepares datasets. Outputs include distillation (fine-tuning smaller models on good traces from stronger models) and generating evals that define agent behavior.

sections.title: Evals as behavior description and the scikit-learn analogy
sections.summary: Trivedy argues you can describe an agent's behavior by showing the evals it was measured against, because agents hill-climb those evals. He draws an analogy to scikit-learn's fit function, describing model-harness-task fit: the modern job is finding good fit functions (auto research, RL methods) and finding good data. The overall ML process hasn't fundamentally changed.

sections.title: Dense feedback, harness engineer-fine-tune-harness engineer cycle
sections.summary: Dense feedback signals are what agents lack most—pass/fail gives no useful signal, while traces hold fine-grained signal agents can read and act on. The iterative improvement cycle: harness engineering gives feedback in about 2 minutes, saturate that ceiling first, then fine-tune to break through, then return to harness engineering. Terminal bench experiments showed agents reading their own traces, proposing experiments, and trying fixes.

sections.title: Continual learning across three axes and sleep-time compute
sections.summary: Continual learning means agents take actions in environments and use that information to update themselves. This must happen across three axes: collecting observational training data, evolving harnesses over time, and managing memory that is not merely append-only. He points to scaling sleep-time compute and dreaming—reading traces over the entire agent life cycle to update agent state.

sections.title: Takeaways
sections.summary: Final takeaways: mining traces gives signals to hill-climb on; turn on tracing and point an agent at it as the easiest first step; open models can make everything smarter and cheaper; continual learning is about operating in environments and integrating data back into agent state; agents will produce more data than ever before and we need research directions to manage that at scale.

demonstrations: Harvey legal benchmark: matched Opus trace judging with an open model at 1-2 orders of magnitude lower cost through harness engineering
LangSplat engine: automates trace mining—reads trace data, finds issues, generates evals, prepares datasets for fine-tuning or analysis
Terminal bench experiment: agents read their own traces, proposed experiments, and tried fixes—demonstrating auto research before the term existed
limitations: Reading traces at scale is expensive—input token cost multiplied by number of traces and average trace size
Long traces (millions of tokens) may not fit in context, requiring external queryable context systems
Harness engineering hits an intelligence ceiling where further prompt tweaking yields diminishing returns
Sparse pass/fail benchmark signals give agents no useful signal to act on
Append-only memory will not scale over year, 5-year, or lifetime agent horizons
